subtype: Joyful, delighted and amused at school age [Interpreting]
passage:
Monday. In the school corridor Payal heard shrieking. Indu's group was jumping around a ball of silver paper, all laughing, and Payal laughed too because they pulled her in. "Everyone's here!" Indu shouted.

Wednesday. Payal heard the group laugh again, but this time Indu pointed at Meera's crooked plait. Meera stood still, her face closed. Payal did not laugh. It felt different.

Friday. When the class giggled at Meera's answer, Payal turned and asked, "Is Meera laughing too?" Meera shook her head. Payal moved to sit beside her. "I'm laughing with you next time," she whispered. Meera nodded a little. 🙂

qa.q: What did Indu's group jump around on Monday?
qa.a: They jumped around a ball of silver paper.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling on Wednesday when the group laughed at Meera's plait, and why did she not laugh?
qa.a: She felt uneasy, because the laughter felt different from Monday's. She noticed that Meera's face closed and that the laugh did not include her.

qa.q: What could Payal do when she hears laughter directed at someone?
qa.a: She can check whether the person is laughing too, as she did, and sit beside them or say something kind.

qa.q: How might Meera feel when Payal sits next to her?
qa.a: Meera may feel relieved that someone noticed she was not enjoying the laugh, though she only nods a little, so she may still be hurt.

grounding: A child learns to tell shared joyful laughter from laughing at someone and checks whether a laugh includes everyone.

subtype: Joyful, delighted and amused at school age [Interpreting]
passage: Beta, come sit. I'm your Madhav Dada, and this is from my school days in Nashik. Our class had a boy called Shankar, tall and quiet. One day the teacher's chair broke and everyone roared. I roared too, I couldn't stop. But when I looked at Shankar he was laughing with his hand over his mouth, a different kind of laugh, worried. Shankar had been sitting on it when it broke. Later I said, "I wasn't laughing at you." He said, "It felt like it." I had to think about that. Since then I look at faces before I join a laugh. Good laughter has room for everyone.

qa.q: What broke in Madhav's story?
qa.a: The teacher's chair broke.

qa.q: What did Shankar's laugh with his hand over his mouth suggest he felt, and what else might it be?
qa.a: It suggested he felt worried or embarrassed, since he had been sitting on the chair when it broke. It might also have been an attempt to laugh along so he would not seem upset.

qa.q: What could a child do after realising a laugh hurt someone?
qa.a: The child can apologise, listen to how it felt, and watch faces before joining a laugh next time, as Madhav learned to do.

qa.q: How does Shankar experience the class laughing?
qa.a: Shankar felt the laugh was aimed at him even though Madhav did not mean it that way, which shows how a laugh can wound without intent.

grounding: An elder recalls learning to tell laughter that includes everyone from laughter that wounds, by looking at the other person's face.

subtype: Joyful, delighted and amused at school age [Interpreting]
passage:
The school bus was packed and steamy because of the rain, and the driver had the radio on loud. When they got off at the gate, Keerthana stepped in a puddle and slid, landing on her bottom with a splash.
Everyone near the gate shouted with laughter. Arnab froze. Was she hurt? Was this bad?
Then he saw Keerthana was laughing hardest of all, flicking mud at her friends. "I'm a mud buffalo!" she yelled. Arnab laughed too.
But a boy kept doing an exaggerated slip, again and again, calling "Mud girl! Mud girl!" Keerthana's grin went stiff. She stood up and wiped her hands on her skirt without looking at anyone.
Arnab stopped laughing. He walked over and held out his handkerchief. "Want this?" She took it and nodded.

qa.q: What did Keerthana call herself after falling?
qa.a: A mud buffalo.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling at first, and how did Arnab tell that it changed?
qa.a: At first Keerthana was laughing hardest and joking, which showed she felt amused and included; when the boy kept mocking, her grin went stiff and she didn't look at anyone, which suggests she felt hurt and embarrassed.

qa.q: What did Arnab do when he noticed the change?
qa.a: He stopped laughing and offered his handkerchief, a small way of standing with her instead of laughing at her.

qa.q: If you were the boy mimicking the slip, what would you want to notice next time?
qa.a: You would want to watch whether the person is still laughing too; once their smile goes stiff, the joke is at them, not with them.

grounding: In the rain at the school gate, a child learns to tell shared laughter from mocking laughter by watching the other person.

subtype: Joyful, delighted and amused at school age [Interpreting]
passage:
At the birthday party in the society hall, little Kamal dove face-first into his cake by accident, trying to blow out candles. Icing everywhere. The kids shrieked with joy. Kamal sat up, eyebrows white, and started giggling so hard he hiccupped. Damini laughed until her eyes watered.
Later, the older kids played charades. When Kamal tried to act "elephant," he said "ele-pant." Some of the big boys fell about laughing and copied him, "ele-pant, ele-pant!"
Kamal went quiet and hid behind his mother's dupatta.
Damini noticed. She stopped laughing and said, "Kamal, you were the best elephant. Show me the trunk again?" Kamal peeked out, then waved his arm like a trunk. This time everyone clapped.

qa.q: What word did Kamal say for elephant?
qa.a: "Ele-pant."

qa.q: What does Kamal hiding behind his mother's dupatta suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt hurt and embarrassed when the big boys laughed at his word, unlike the cake moment when he joined the laughter.

qa.q: What did Damini do that helped?
qa.a: She turned the attention to what Kamal did well and invited him back into the game, so the laughter became with him instead of at him.

qa.q: How might the big boys see the laughter differently from Kamal?
qa.a: They probably thought it was just funny, not noticing that Kamal had stopped laughing and felt left out.

grounding: At a party, a child notices the difference between laughing with and laughing at someone and helps include him.

subtype: Joyful, delighted and amused at school age [Interpreting]
passage:
"Jasleen, you laughed today when I said 'pee-zza' in English class."
"Everyone laughed, Devika. It was funny, na? I thought you were joking!"
"I wasn't. That's how my Dadi says it."
"Oh." Jasleen's face went pink. "But you smiled."
"I smiled so no one would see I wanted to cry."
"I didn't know. When you laughed at my wrong answer last week, I laughed too."
"That was different. We were both laughing. Today it was everyone laughing at me."
Jasleen was quiet for a moment. "How was I supposed to tell?"
Devika shrugged. "Look if the person is laughing with their eyes, not just their mouth. Or just ask."
Jasleen nodded. "I'm sorry. Next time I'll ask."
"Okay." Devika smiled, and this time it reached her eyes.

qa.q: How did Devika say the word in English class?
qa.a: 'Pee-zza'.

qa.q: Why did Devika smile in class?
qa.a: Devika smiled to hide feeling embarrassed and upset, so no one would see she wanted to cry.

qa.q: What tip did Devika give for telling kind laughter from hurtful laughter?
qa.a: Look at whether the person is laughing with their eyes, not just their mouth, or simply ask.

qa.q: How did Jasleen see the class laughter at first?
qa.a: Jasleen thought it was fun and shared, and didn't realise Devika was hurt behind her smile.

grounding: Two friends talk about how to tell laughing with someone from laughing at them, and how a smile can hide hurt.

subtype: Joyful, delighted and amused at school age [Interpreting]
passage: I'm Binita, and last week I learned that two kinds of laughing can sound almost the same. First, Vishal's chair squeaked like a duck every time he leaned back. He did it on purpose, quack, quack, and the whole class, Vishal loudest of all, shouted with laughter. It felt like one big happy noise. Then on Friday Vishal was reading aloud and his voice cracked on "photosynthesis". A few kids at the back snorted and copied the crack. This time Vishal wasn't laughing. His ears turned red and he read faster. I stopped laughing. At break I told him the chair duck was the best thing all week, and he smiled a little. Now I look at the person's face before I join in.

qa.q: Which word did Vishal's voice crack on?
qa.a: "Photosynthesis".

qa.q: Why did Binita stop laughing on Friday?
qa.a: Binita felt uncomfortable and sorry for Vishal on seeing his red ears and hurried reading, and understood the laughter was now at him, not with him.

qa.q: What habit did Binita take away from the week?
qa.a: Looking at the person's face before joining a laugh, to check it includes everyone.

qa.q: How was the chair-duck laughter different for Vishal?
qa.a: Vishal chose that joke and laughed loudest, so it felt like connection; the voice crack was not his choice, so the copying stung.

grounding: It shows a child learning to tell shared laughter from laughter at someone by checking whether the person is laughing too.
